claims.text: Adjusting relative elemental composition, or substitutional alloying, can be used to tune non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Changing the proportion of magnetic to nonmagnetic 3d elements systematically modifies exchange interactions.
Composition-induced changes in exchange interactions shift the magnetic ordering temperature.
Composition-induced changes in exchange interactions alter the magnetocaloric response.
CoCrFeMnNi is an example of a high-entropy-alloy system based on 3d transition metals.
A non-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy exhibits a balance of magnetic interactions.
Co and Fe are high-moment elements relative to Cr, Mn, or Ni in the proposed alloy context.
Changing elemental ratios changes the local chemical environment and produces local lattice distortions.
Changing alloy composition can alter phase fractions.
Changing composition modifies local magnetic-moment distributions.
Modified exchange interactions and local magnetic moments shift the Curie temperature.
Modified exchange interactions and local magnetic moments change the magnitude and temperature dependence of the magnetocaloric effect by changing magnetic entropy near the transition.
Systematic composition adjustment will produce a systematic shift in Curie temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
Systematic composition adjustment will alter magnetic entropy change relative to the baseline alloy.
Increasing Co or Fe content will enhance the magnetocaloric response near the tailored transition temperature.
The tuning effect is significant only within compositional ranges that preserve a single-phase solid solution.
Large composition changes can cause phase separation or other structural instabilities.
Phase separation or structural instability can mask or alter magnetocaloric behavior.
The effects of composition on magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior may be nonlinear because of interplay between local structural distortions and magnetic interactions.
